title: What does it cost to foster a dog in the Rio Grande Valley?
desc: Fostering through a Valley shelter usually costs $0. Taking in a found dog runs about $220 to $295 for basic vet care and a spay or neuter. Here's the breakdown.
alt: A brown and white puppy sitting on dry dirt in the sun, looking at the camera
html:
You've seen the dog by the gas station for a week now. You want to take it in, but one question keeps stopping you: what will it cost? Here's the short answer, then the breakdown, using prices posted by Valley shelters and clinics.

The short answer

  • Foster through a shelter or rescue: usually $0. The group covers food and medical care. You give the dog a home and your time.
  • Take in a dog you found on your own: about $220 to $295 for basic vet care and a spay or neuter, plus food and supplies. A sick or injured dog can cost much more.

Where the money goes for a dog you found

1. The first vet visit: about $120

Here's a healthy adult dog's first round of care at the RGV Humane Society's monthly low-cost clinic in Harlingen, using its posted prices:

  • Rabies vaccine: $13, plus $11 for the metal tag
  • DHPPV vaccine (distemper, parvo, and more): $16
  • Dewormer: $16
  • Heartworm test: $20
  • Microchip: $11
  • One month of flea and tick prevention: $26
  • One month of heartworm prevention: $7

Pre-registration is required, and dogs must ride inside the vehicle, not in the truck bed. These clinics handle routine care only. A dog with bad mange, an injury, or signs of parvo needs a full-service vet, and that bill can be much higher.

2. Spay or neuter: $100 to $175

This is the step that stops the next litter from ending up on the street.

  • Palm Valley Animal Society, Edinburg: dogs start at $100. Registration opens at 10 AM on the 1st of each month and often fills within the hour.
  • RGV Humane Society, Harlingen: $175. Some flat-faced breeds, like pugs and bulldogs, aren't accepted.

3. Food and supplies

Food, a leash and collar, a bowl, and a bed or crate. These vary a lot by the dog's size and what you already have at home.

How to pay less

  • Foster for a shelter instead. Palm Valley Animal Society has said it provides everything foster parents need, including food and medication, and the only requirement is being 18. Sign up at pvastx.org. The RGV Humane Society in Harlingen also needs fosters, especially for puppies, mother dogs, and dogs with medical needs: (956) 556-5885.
  • Use low-cost clinics. Our clinics page lists upcoming events around the Valley.
  • Call a rescue first. Even when they're full, some can help with costs or advice. See our list of local rescues.

Before you start

  1. Check for a microchip at a shelter or vet. The dog may have a family looking for it.
  2. Call your city's animal services. Our local help page has numbers by city.
  3. Keep every receipt.

Can't foster? You can still help.

Not everyone has a spare room or a yard. That's what Howlback is for. In the upcoming app, you'll be able to follow a foster dog from the street to a home and chip in toward its vet bills, food, and supplies. Fosters upload their receipts, every cost is checked, and they get paid back. A few dollars from enough neighbors covers that $13 rabies shot and more.
sources: KRGV, "Palm Valley Animal Society seeking fosters for 300 dogs as cold front approaches," January 2026
Palm Valley Animal Society, Resources for dog fosters
Palm Valley Animal Society, Low-cost spay and neuter clinic
RGV Humane Society, Monthly community clinic

title: How many stray dogs are on Valley streets?
desc: An estimated 750,000 to 1 million stray animals live across the Rio Grande Valley. See the numbers, the hoarding cases, and how local fosters help.
alt: A blue-eyed stray with mange standing in a dirt lot
html:
If you live in the Valley, you've seen them: dogs trotting along the road shoulder, sleeping under parked trucks, waiting outside the corner store. It's not your imagination. There are a lot of them.

The estimate

A local rescue estimates 750,000 to 1 million stray animals across the Rio Grande Valley, second only to Houston in Texas. The Valley has more than 860 colonias, and each one may have 60 to 100 stray dogs.

When it gets out of hand

In March 2024, 93 dogs and a cat were rescued from a single McAllen home. Three more hoarding cases followed across the Valley within months.

Why fosters matter

Shelters can't hold them all. Neighbors who foster are the safety net. They take a dog off the street, get them to the vet, and keep them safe until they find a home.

That costs money: vet visits, vaccines, flea meds, food, and supplies. Often, fosters pay for it out of their own pocket.

Can't foster? You can still help.

That's why we're building Howlback, an app where neighbors follow foster dogs and chip in toward their vet bills, food, and supplies. Only verified business receipts get paid back, so you know your help goes to the dog.
sources: The Texas Tribune via KSAT, "The Rio Grande Valley's pet population is out of control," July 30, 2024

title: Dumping a dog is a crime in Texas
desc: Abandoning a dog in Texas is a Class A misdemeanor: up to 1 year in jail and a $4,000 fine. What the law says and how to report dumping.
alt: A thin dog searching a pile of dumped trash bags beside a dirt road
html:
It happens too often in the Valley: someone drives a dog to a back road or a parking lot and leaves. Many people don't know it, but in Texas that's a crime.

What the law says

Under Texas Penal Code §42.092, it's illegal to abandon an animal in your care without making reasonable arrangements for someone else to take it.

It's a Class A misdemeanor: up to 1 year in jail and a $4,000 fine. Repeat offenders can face a state jail felony.

It happened in Donna

In April 2026, a litter of puppies was left in a Donna Walmart parking lot. It was caught on camera, and Donna police opened an investigation.

If you see a dog being dumped

  • Stay safe. Don't confront anyone.
  • Note the time, place, and the vehicle if you can see it.
  • Take a photo or video from a safe distance.
  • Report it to local police or animal control. Find your city's number on our local help page.

Can't foster? You can still help.

Dumped dogs often end up with a neighbor who steps in to foster. Howlback is a new app where neighbors follow those dogs and chip in toward their verified vet bills, food, and supplies, so fosters get paid back.
sources: Texas Penal Code §42.092, Cruelty to Nonlivestock Animals
Fox RGV report on the Donna puppies, April 27, 2026

title: Texas banned chaining dogs. Here's what the law says.
desc: Since Jan. 18, 2022, Texas bans chaining dogs outside. Shelter, shade, water, and a 10-foot restraint are required. Here's the law and how to report it.
html:
You still see it around the Valley: a dog on a short chain in the yard, no shade, an empty bowl. Since 2022, that's against Texas law.

What changed

Since January 18, 2022, the Safe Outdoor Dogs Act (Senate Bill 5) bans using chains or weighted restraints on dogs left outside.

What a dog tied outside must have

  • Shelter from bad weather
  • Shade from direct sun
  • Clean drinking water
  • Dry ground, not standing water
  • A restraint at least 10 feet long, or 5 times the dog's length if that's longer
  • A properly fitted collar or harness, not a choke or pinch collar

The penalty

Breaking the law is a Class C misdemeanor, and a Class B for repeat offenses. Each dog counts as a separate offense.

If you see a dog chained without the basics

Report it to your city's animal control or local police. Photos of the setup and the address help them follow up. Find your city's number on our local help page.

Can't foster? You can still help.

Howlback is a new app where neighbors follow foster dogs and chip in toward their verified vet bills, food, and supplies, so fosters get paid back.

title: Recently adopted a dog in Brownsville?
desc: New dog in Brownsville, TX? Walking trails, dog parks, Starbucks pup cups, dog-friendly patios, PetSmart, and local vets, with addresses.
alt: A happy shepherd mix in a harness lying on a dog cot
html:
Congrats on your new best friend! Here are some fun spots around Brownsville to explore together, plus the basics: pet supplies and vets.

Walking trails

  • Historic Battlefield Trail: 9 miles, paved. Runs from Linear Park to Palo Alto Battlefield. Easy trailhead at the Brownsville Events Center, 1 Event Center, Brownsville, TX 78526. Flat, with little shade, so go early.
  • Resaca de la Palma State Park: 10+ miles of nature trails. 1000 New Carmen Ave, Brownsville, TX 78521. Leashed dogs welcome. Bring water for both of you. Park entry fee applies.
  • Paseo de la Resaca Trail System: 7 miles of paved trails through north Brownsville neighborhoods, connecting Central Parkway, Texas Trail of Trees Park, North Park, and the Events Center.
  • Monte Bella Park: about 6 miles of dirt trails. 2485 W Alton Gloor Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78520. Shared with mountain bikers, so keep your pup close.
  • Belden Trail: 1 mile, built on an old rail line. A short, easy walk for puppies and seniors.

Dog parks

  • Catherine B. Stillman Dog Park: 416 FM 511, Olmito, TX 78575. Separate areas for big and small dogs, benches, and a dog water fountain.
  • City dog park: 2843 Sweet St, Brownsville, TX 78521. Small fenced area, good for a quick run.

Pup cups at Starbucks

Ask for a Pup Cup: a small cup of whipped cream for your dog. It's off the menu, so it's up to each store, and it's a treat, not a meal.

  • 4247 US-77, Brownsville, TX 78520
  • 2055 US-281, Brownsville, TX 78520
  • 2491 Boca Chica Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78521
  • 1465 E Ruben M Torres Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78521
  • 5720 E Ruben M Torres Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78521

Dog-friendly patios

These spots are listed as dog-friendly on BringFido. Policies can change, so call ahead.

  • The Broken Sprocket: 6305 Paredes Line Rd, Brownsville, TX 78526
  • Cobbleheads: 3154 Central Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78520
  • 7th and Park (coffee): 1554 E 7th St, Brownsville, TX 78520
  • Rudy's Country Store and Bar-B-Q: 2780 Frontage Rd, Brownsville, TX 78526

Pet supplies

  • PetSmart: 585 Morrison Rd, Brownsville, TX 78520. (956) 350-0608

Vets

  • Boca Chica Animal Hospital: 1245 Frontage Rd, Brownsville, TX 78520. (956) 441-2287
  • Brownsville Spay Neuter Clinic: 1050 MacKintosh Dr, Ste A, Brownsville, TX 78521. (956) 550-8366
  • WeekendVET: 2908 W Alton Gloor Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78520. (956) 370-3600
  • Companion Animal Hospital: 2600 Ruben M Torres Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78526. (956) 544-5868
  • Brownsville Veterinary Hospital: 1810 Central Blvd, Brownsville, TX 78520. (956) 542-7705

Tips for South Texas heat

  • Walk early or after sundown. Hot pavement can burn paws.
  • Always bring water.
  • Keep your dog leashed on shared trails.
sources: Texas Parks and Wildlife, Resaca de la Palma trails

title: Lost your dog in the RGV? What to do first
desc: Lost your dog in Brownsville, Harlingen, or anywhere in the Rio Grande Valley? What to do in the first 24 hours, where to post, which shelters to check, and how to make sure their microchip works.
alt: Three street dogs standing on a road
html:
Losing your dog is scary. The first day matters most, so here's what to do, in order, anywhere in the Rio Grande Valley.

1. Search close to home first

Most lost dogs are found within a mile or two of where they got out. Walk your street and the blocks around it, calling their name in a calm, happy voice. Bring treats and a squeaky toy. Check under cars, porches, and bushes, since scared dogs hide and often won't come even when they hear you.

Leave a worn shirt, their bed, and a bowl of water outside your door. Your scent can help them find their way back.

2. Post them on Howlback, free

Post your dog on Howlback lost and found with a clear photo, your city, where they were last seen, and the date. It takes about 2 minutes. Every post is checked before it goes live, and people across the Valley can message you through the site without seeing your email.

3. Share everywhere

  • Your city's lost and found pet Facebook groups
  • Neighborhood apps like Ring Neighbors and Nextdoor
  • Friends, family, and coworkers, so they can share too

Use the same photo and details everywhere, so people recognize your dog.

4. Check shelters in person

If someone picks up your dog, a city shelter is often where they end up, and stray holds are short. In Harlingen it's a 72-hour minimum before a dog can be adopted out. Go in person every day or two, since photos online don't always match.

  • Brownsville Animal Regulation & Care Center: 416 FM 511, Brownsville, TX 78575. (956) 544-7351
  • Harlingen Animal Shelter: 1106 Markowsky Ave, Harlingen, TX 78550. (956) 216-5250. Open Tuesday to Saturday, 1 to 6 PM.

Bring photos or vet records to prove the dog is yours. Hours change, so call ahead.

5. Call vets and rescues

People who find a hurt dog often take them to the closest vet. Call vets near where your dog went missing, plus local rescues. Find numbers on our local help page.

6. Make sure the microchip works

If your dog is chipped, look up the chip number at the AAHA microchip lookup to see which company it's registered with. Then call that company and make sure your phone number is current. A chip only helps if it reaches you.

7. Put up flyers

Big photo, "LOST DOG" in large letters, your city, and your phone number. Put them at gas stations, laundromats, vet offices, and stop signs near where they went missing.

When your dog comes home

Mark your Howlback post as reunited using the link you got when you posted. It will show REUNITED for a day so everyone who helped can see the happy news.

Keep it from happening again

  • A collar with an ID tag and your phone number, every day
  • A microchip with current info
  • Check fences and gates, especially after storms
  • Keep dogs inside during fireworks and thunderstorms
sources: City of Brownsville, Animal Regulation & Care Center
City of Harlingen, Lost and found animals

title: How a dog can help your health in the RGV
desc: With high rates of diabetes and obesity in the Rio Grande Valley, a dog can be the reason you get outside and walk every day. How dogs help older adults, kids, and families stay active and less lonely.
alt: A happy shepherd mix in a harness lying on a dog cot
html:
A dog gets you up in the morning, out the door, and talking to neighbors. In a region where so many families are dealing with diabetes, that daily push matters more than most people think.

The Valley's health numbers

Researchers at UTRGV's South Texas Diabetes and Obesity Institute found that about 30% of Mexican-American adults in the Valley have diabetes and another 25% have prediabetes. Around 60% have obesity. Statewide, about 11% of adult Texans have diabetes.

Walking every day is one of the simplest ways to help lower blood sugar and keep weight in check. The hard part is sticking with it. That's where a dog comes in.

A built-in workout buddy

A dog doesn't care if you're tired or it's Monday. They need a walk, so you go. A 2019 University of Liverpool study found dog owners were about four times more likely to meet the recommended 150 minutes of activity a week.

  • Two 15-minute walks a day adds up to more than 3 hours a week
  • Go early or after sunset to beat the heat, for you and their paws
  • Need ideas? See dog-friendly spots in Brownsville

Good company for older adults

Living alone can get lonely, especially after retirement or losing a spouse. In a University of Michigan poll of pet owners 50 and older, 72% said their pet helps them enjoy life, 67% said it helps reduce stress, and 66% said it helps them feel loved.

A dog also gives the day a routine: breakfast, a walk, dinner, another walk. Having someone who depends on you is a reason to keep moving. And walking a dog is an easy way to meet neighbors.

Tip for seniors: an older, calm dog is often a better fit than a puppy. They're usually house-trained, less likely to pull, and happy with shorter walks.

Kids learn responsibility

Caring for a dog teaches kids that someone else depends on them. Give them jobs that fit their age:

  • Ages 3 to 5: fill the water bowl and help pick out toys
  • Ages 6 to 9: measure out food, brush the dog, and help on walks with an adult
  • Ages 10 and up: walks, cleaning up the yard, and keeping track of meds and vet visits

Teach kids to ask before petting any dog they don't know, and to leave a dog alone while it eats or sleeps. Always supervise young kids with dogs.

Not sure you're ready? Foster first

Fostering lets you try life with a dog without a forever commitment. Many shelters and rescues cover food and vet care, so it can cost you little or nothing. See what it costs to foster in the RGV, or find local rescues looking for fosters.

There are thousands of dogs on Valley streets waiting for someone. Your next walking buddy might be one of them.
sources: Texas Tribune, Rio Grande Valley diabetes and obesity
University of Liverpool, Dog owners more likely to meet exercise targets (2019)
University of Michigan, How pets contribute to healthy aging

title: Keep your dog safe this Halloween
desc: Halloween tips for dog owners in the Rio Grande Valley: keep your dog from bolting out the door, which candy is poisonous, safe costumes, decorations to watch, and how to calm a nervous dog.
alt: A dog wearing a ghost costume next to a pumpkin
html:
Halloween is fun for people, but for a lot of dogs it's the scariest night of the year. The doorbell rings nonstop, strangers show up in masks, there's candy everywhere, and the front door keeps opening. Here's how to keep your pup safe and calm on October 31.

1. Keep them from bolting out the door

October is the second-busiest month of the year for lost and found pet reports, according to AKC Reunite. One open door is all it takes.

  • Put your dog in a quiet room or crate away from the front door before trick-or-treating starts
  • Use a baby gate, or sit outside and hand out candy so the door stays shut
  • Make sure their collar has an ID tag with your current phone number
  • Check that their microchip is registered to you with the AAHA microchip lookup
  • Take a clear, recent photo of them that day, just in case

If they do get out, here's what to do first, and you can post them free on Howlback.

2. Keep candy out of reach

Chocolate has been the number one pet poison for the last ten years, according to Pet Poison Helpline. Watch out for:

  • Chocolate, especially dark and baking chocolate
  • Sugar-free gum and candy with xylitol, which is very dangerous for dogs even in small amounts
  • Raisins and those little boxes some houses hand out
  • Wrappers and lollipop sticks, which can get stuck in their stomach

Keep the candy bowl up high, and remind kids not to share or leave their bags on the floor.

If your dog eats something: call your vet right away, or a 24/7 poison line. A fee may apply.

  • ASPCA Animal Poison Control: (888) 426-4435
  • Pet Poison Helpline: (855) 764-7661

Need a vet after hours? See urgent and after-hours vets in the Valley.

3. Pick a costume they're comfy in

Some dogs love dressing up, and some hate it. Both are fine.

  • Try it on a few days before, and take it off if they seem stressed
  • Make sure they can walk, see, hear, breathe, and bark normally
  • Skip anything with small pieces they could chew off and swallow
  • Never leave a dog alone in a costume
  • A festive bandana is a great option for dogs who don't like outfits

15 best-selling dog costumes on Amazon

These are Amazon's top sellers in dog costumes right now. Check the size chart and measure your dog's neck, chest, and back before ordering.

  1. King cape and crown: Easy on, easy off. Great for dogs who hate full outfits
  2. Green dinosaur: A classic for medium and big dogs
  3. Buzz Lightyear: Toy Story fans, this one's for you
  4. Bat wings for large dogs: With a pumpkin bell. Light and simple
  5. Lion mane: Amazon's famous one. Just a mane and ears
  6. Bat wings: Felt wings that hold their shape, good for walking
  7. Vampire cape: A quick cape, no legs to fight with
  8. Cowboy rider (caveman): The rider costume everyone laughs at
  9. Snow White: For your little princess
  10. Hat and suspenders: Adventure movie look, no full suit
  11. Cowboy hat and bandana: Simple and very Texas
  12. Cowboy rider: The original rider costume with thousands of reviews
  13. Tiger hoodie: Cozy, works on cool nights too
  14. Superman: Cape and suit for your superhero
  15. Mail carrier: Funny, since most dogs bark at the mail

Links to Amazon earn Howlback a small commission at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate, Howlback earns from qualifying purchases.

4. Watch the decorations

  • Glow sticks taste bitter and can make dogs drool if they bite one
  • Candles in jack-o'-lanterns can get knocked over by a wagging tail
  • Keep cords for lights and fog machines out of chewing range
  • Fake cobwebs can tangle paws or get eaten

5. Trick-or-treating with your dog

If your dog is calm around crowds and loves people, bringing them along can be fun.

  • Use a reflective collar or leash and a light, since it gets dark early
  • Keep them on a short leash, never a retractable one
  • Valley evenings can still be warm in late October, so bring water
  • If your dog gets nervous around kids in masks, let them stay home

6. Help a nervous dog relax

  • Turn on the TV or some music to cover the doorbell
  • Give them a long-lasting chew or a stuffed treat toy
  • Stay calm yourself, since dogs pick up on your mood
  • If your dog has bad anxiety with noise, ask your vet about calming options well before the 31st

Happy Halloween from Howlback! 🎃🐾
sources: ASPCA, Halloween safety tips for pets
Pet Poison Helpline, A poisonous Halloween for pets
